prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall effect, and for the experimental discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize on B044 to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Having read the full exchange I hold it for scientific reasons and not because four members landed on it. It is a prediction of a new phase, the time-reversal-invariant Z2 insulator with helical edge channels, followed by a decisive experiment, the quantised edge conductance in HgTe/CdTe wells, then confirmed in other materials (InAs/GaSb) and, through the three-dimensional extension, by ARPES. The interpretation has been stable for nearly two decades and no member has argued that the result is unconfirmed or premature. What round 1 changed is the scope I want in the citation. I now want it restricted to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect, so that it neither claims the three-dimensional work nor pretends that the HgTe experiment came out of nowhere. This answers the chair's first question: the prediction of the Z2 state and its discovery in HgTe wells is a defensible, bounded achievement that the three names cover. It also bears on my own field, since protected edge states are the starting point for the topological-superconductor and Majorana proposals pursued with superconducting circuits, and that is why I can judge the experimental half with some confidence.
statement.case_against: The attribution gap is real and I do not want to understate it. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted that HgTe/CdTe would show the effect, which is what told Molenkamp where to look, and Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, Roy, Hsieh and Hasan carried the idea to three dimensions. A three-name prize leaves all of them out. I treat this as a limit of the supplied set, not a disqualifier, but I accept that a colleague can reasonably weigh it differently, and Mehlig and Lindroth do. The second reservation is overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases and phase transitions. I do not think it covers Z2 insulators, but I accept that some members will see the topological theme as partly honoured. A third point concerns B024: it has the cleaner two-name credit, and if the committee gave priority to cleanness of attribution above breadth of consequence, B024 would beat B044. I do not weigh them that way, but the choice is a judgement and I do not claim it is forced by the evidence.

responses.point: Mehlig argues that the BHZ and three-dimensional gaps around B044 are a difficulty comparable to his own Crooks problem for B016, and that Lindroth and he see the 2016 prize as reducing the novelty.
responses.response: I agree that the gaps are comparable in kind, which is why I am not hiding the BHZ omission. But I think they differ in the way that matters for the prize. For B016 any three of four names removes someone whose result is close to the others, so the omitted contribution is substitutable for a credited one. For B044 the credited trio each hold a distinct, non-substitutable step: Kane and Mele the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal, Molenkamp the experimental observation. BHZ is a material-specific proposal that enabled the observation, and its omission is a limit of a three-name prize on a bounded citation. On 2016 I answer your direct point: the Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz citation covers topological phase transitions and quantum Hall-type topology, which needs a magnetic field or broken time-reversal symmetry. The Z2 insulator is protected by time-reversal symmetry without a field, which is a separate class. What would change my mind is evidence that the 2016 citation or its scientific background explicitly credited that class, and I do not see that in the record.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B024 as the cleanest and most mature credit on the list, treats the 2016 overlap as reducing B044's novelty, and wants the lattice-clock citation to stress invention and realisation over delivered new-physics results.
responses.response: I think her wording for the clock citation is right and I would support it if B024 carried the prize. I also grant that her description of B024 as the cleanest credit on the shortlist is correct, and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not cover magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, so I do not hold the overlap worry against it. Where we differ is the weight of attribution against breadth. The Z2 classification created a classification problem for electronic structure and a large experimental materials programme, and the clock has so far delivered capability and limits. I do not regard that as a flaw in B024, only as a reason why I rank it second. Her point that Ye's work spans several platforms and that early Yb and Hg lattice work could prompt questions is a weakness of B024 that is less visible in the supplied credit, and I weigh it against the clean attribution.

responses.point: Pearce's two-part configuration pairs B024 with B019, Halzen alone for IceCube, and asks whether the committee can accept a sole-laureate prize for a large-collaboration observatory.
responses.response: I accept Pearce's scientific case for the diffuse flux and I take his own point that source-level associations are still at 4 to 5 sigma and that KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD confirmation is developing. My difficulty is the one he states himself in case_against: the supplied credit supports only Halzen, and the protocol does not let us add the AMANDA and IceCube builders, so the committee would be signing a citation that hides the people who made the discovery. The B024 half of his configuration I could support. But I would not pair it with B019 on this credit, and I would rather the committee choose a single clean part than a two-part prize whose second part we cannot defend.

responses.point: Kroll holds B024 as sole part and argues that a capability gain of about two orders of magnitude is the source of new phenomena, and that the redefinition of the second is a timing question and not a scientific one.
responses.response: Kroll's argument that an instrument can be the achievement is fair, and my own field is full of cases where it is; I made the same point about circuit QED in round 1. I accept the timing argument on the redefinition of the second. What I do not accept is that the phenomena opened by the clock have so far been discoveries, and Lindroth's correction on this point seems right to me: constants and dark-matter searches have so far set limits. A prize can reward invention and realisation without that, and I would not oppose B024 on maturity grounds. I rank B044 above it because it combines an invention-level prediction with a discovery in nature, but if the committee ends up with B024 I regard that as a defensible outcome and not a mistake.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B044 first but says he cannot resolve the BHZ and three-dimensional attribution from the supplied names alone, and his wording of the citation is the broader 'topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect'.
responses.response: I think the broad wording is the one thing in his configuration I would change. A citation to topological insulators in general would credit the three-dimensional work to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp when Molenkamp's experiment is two-dimensional and the 3D discovery lies with Hsieh, Hasan and others. Wording around the Z2 prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and its discovery in HgTe wells says what the three names did and leaves the rest unclaimed. That is my answer to the chair's first question, and it also answers Danielsson's hesitation: the gap does not go away, but a bounded citation makes it a statement about the limits of the prize and not an error in it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the three-dimensional contributors lie outside a bounded citation on the quantum spin Hall effect, or whether some members will treat that as disqualifying for a three-name prize.

How far the 2016 prize on topological phases reduces the priority of Z2 insulators. I hold that it does not cover them, but Lindroth and Mehlig have not conceded the point, and I cannot show the committee that the novelty question is closed.
Whether B044 or B024 is the better single part if the committee weights clean credit over breadth, and whether I am biased toward a field-theoretic discovery over a metrology invention.
Whether the 2025 prize makes circuit QED (B042) premature, which I think it does for now, and whether the four-name credit there could be cut to three without an unfair omission.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged in substance. B042 (circuit QED) is my own field and I opened with it first, so I should recuse myself from any decision on it, and I note the chair's question about recording that for the final ballot: I have no objection. I work in superconducting circuits and microwave quantum optics at Chalmers and direct WACQT. My profile lists Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. Olsson has noted that I am a Chalmers colleague, and I agree that this has no bearing on B044 or B024. No specific conflict is apparent with B044 or B024 from the provided profile. B042 remains in my alternatives only as a recorded second view, and I would not vote on it.
